kurz: How Social Security, employer plans and personal savings fit together in the US, how each is taxed at the federal level and how tightly each ties up the money.

bloecke.md:
Retirement income in the United States is often described as a three-legged stool. The first leg is Social Security, the second is employer plans such as the 401(k) or a traditional pension, and the third is personal savings. The picture is not a legal category and does not set an order of priority. The Social Security Administration's historians note that the origin of the metaphor is unclear. It is useful because it shows that each leg carries part of the weight and that the stool wobbles when one leg is short.

The tax code sorts the same money a second time, by tax treatment. Money is either **pre-tax** (deductible now, taxed on withdrawal), **Roth** (taxed now, tax-free on withdrawal) or **taxable** (no deduction, income taxed along the way). The more tax help an account offers, the more rules apply to it, for example an age limit for withdrawals, required minimum distributions or contribution limits. The commitment is looser than in many other countries, because there are exceptions and Roth contributions can be taken out again. Savers who look only at the tax break still accept restrictions that are hard to undo later.

bloecke.titel: Tax help and access across the three legs
bloecke.unter: From the bottom leg to the top, the money becomes more freely available, while the lifelong and inflation-protected character of the payout disappears.

stufen.text: IRA, HSA, taxable brokerage account, savings, home equity. Limited tax help in IRAs and HSAs, none in a taxable account, which is available at any time.
401(k), 403(b), 457(b), Thrift Savings Plan, traditional pension. Pre-tax or Roth contributions, often an employer match, access as a rule from 59½.
Mandatory payroll tax, lifelong benefit adjusted for inflation, spouse and survivor benefits. No account and no access to capital, payable from 62 at the earliest.

bloecke.md:
## Social Security (leg 1)

Almost every employee and self-employed person pays into Social Security. In 2026, employees pay 6.2% of wages up to the taxable maximum of $184,500 and employers pay the same again. Self-employed people pay both shares, 12.4%, through the self-employment tax. Medicare tax of 1.45% each comes on top and has no ceiling. In return, workers earn credits and an entitlement to a lifelong monthly benefit that is adjusted to inflation every year. Spouses, divorced spouses after at least ten years of marriage, survivors and minor children can receive benefits based on the same record.

The entitlement cannot be cashed out, borrowed against or left to heirs as capital. It is largely protected from creditors (42 U.S.C. § 407), with exceptions for federal taxes, other federal debts, child support and alimony. The lesson "Social Security basics" explains how the benefit is calculated.

bloecke.titel: What the payroll tax pays for
bloecke.md: An employee earning $60,000 in 2026 pays 6.2% Social Security tax, that is $3,720, and her employer pays another $3,720. Together, $7,440 a year flows into the system. For Medicare, each side pays a further $870. Unlike contributions to a 401(k), the employee share of these taxes is not deductible for federal income tax. The $3,720 is therefore paid out of income that has already been taxed. Self-employed people may deduct half of their self-employment tax when calculating adjusted gross income.

## Pre-tax, Roth and taxable money

The tax code treats retirement money in three ways, regardless of which leg it belongs to.

- **Pre-tax (tax-deferred):** contributions reduce taxable income today, earnings grow untaxed, and every dollar withdrawn is ordinary income. Traditional 401(k) deferrals and deductible Traditional IRA contributions work this way.
- **Roth:** contributions come from taxed income, and qualified withdrawals, including all growth, are tax-free. Roth 401(k) and Roth IRA work this way.
- **Taxable:** there is no deduction. Interest and dividends are taxed each year, and gains when you sell. Long-term gains and qualified dividends are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% depending on taxable income (26 U.S.C. § 1(h)), plus the 3.8% net investment income tax above $200,000 of income for single filers and $250,000 for joint filers.

The value of postponing tax comes from two sources: the [[Tax deferral effect|tax deferral effect]] on earnings and the difference between the tax rate today and in retirement.

bloecke.formel: Final value pre-tax / Final value Roth = (1 - tR) / (1 - tW)
bloecke.erklaerung: With the same pre-tax amount, the same investment and the same costs, the comparison between a pre-tax account and a Roth account depends only on the two marginal tax rates. If they are equal, both end with exactly the same amount. A taxable account falls behind both, because its earnings are taxed along the way or on sale.
variablen: marginal tax rate while working, when the contribution is made
marginal tax rate in retirement, when the money is withdrawn
bloecke.beispiel: With tW = 22% and tR = 12%, the result is 0.88 / 0.78 = 1.13, so the pre-tax account ends around 13% ahead. With 22% in both phases, the ratio is exactly 1.00. If the rate rises from 12% to 24%, it is 0.76 / 0.88 = 0.86, and the Roth account comes out ahead.

bloecke.md:
## Employer plans (leg 2)

Most private employers that offer a plan today offer a defined contribution plan, usually a 401(k). Public schools and nonprofits use the 403(b), state and local governments the 457(b), and federal employees and the military the Thrift Savings Plan. Employees decide how much of their pay to defer, up to $24,500 in 2026, and many employers add a match. The assets are held in trust, separate from the employer's own money. Traditional defined benefit pensions, which promise a monthly amount for life, are still common in the public sector but have become rare in private companies. Benefits from private pensions are insured up to statutory limits by the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC).

Deferrals to a 401(k) reduce income tax, but not Social Security and Medicare tax. Withdrawals before age 59½ generally cost an additional 10% tax on top of income tax. Exceptions exist, for example after leaving the employer in or after the year you turn 55. From age 73 (75 for those born in 1960 or later), required minimum distributions must be taken from pre-tax accounts each year. The lesson "401(k), 403(b) and the employer match" covers the details.

Pre-tax money is not your money alone. Part of every balance belongs to the IRS, and you do not know today at what rate it will be collected. Withdrawals are ordinary income, they can make up to 85% of Social Security benefits taxable and they can raise Medicare premiums through the income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA). Required minimum distributions force withdrawals even when you do not need the money. Most states also tax withdrawals, some do not, and moving to another state in retirement changes the result. Finally, tax rates are set by Congress and can change during the decades in which the money is invested.

## Personal savings (leg 3)

The third leg covers everything you save on your own. Individual retirement accounts (IRAs) allow $7,500 a year in 2026, plus $1,100 from age 50, as Traditional or Roth. A health savings account (HSA) can serve as an additional retirement account if you have a qualifying high-deductible health plan. Everything else goes into a taxable brokerage account, a savings account or home equity. These assets have no age limit, no contribution limit and no required withdrawals. Heirs also receive a step-up in basis for assets in a taxable account, so the gains accrued until death are never taxed as income.

Which IRA suits whom is explained in the lesson "Traditional and Roth IRAs". Further options such as the HSA, the Saver's Credit and plans for the self-employed follow in "Beyond the IRA and 401(k)".

bloecke.titel: $4,000 of gross pay after 25 years in four accounts (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: On the left is the net cost today, on the right the amount available after federal income tax, in each case before fund costs and state taxes.

bloecke.md:
The calculation assumes 25 years at a return of 5% a year, a federal marginal tax rate of 22% today and 12% in retirement. State income tax, fund costs and the taxation of dividends along the way are left out. Social Security and Medicare tax are due in all four cases and therefore do not change the comparison.

- **Traditional 401(k):** the full $4,000 goes in untaxed and grows to $13,545. After 12% tax on withdrawal, around $11,920 remains. The net cost today is $4,000 minus 22% tax saved, that is $3,120.
- **With a 50% match:** the employer adds $2,000, so $6,000 grows to $20,318 and around $17,880 remains after tax.
- **Roth IRA:** after 22% tax, $3,120 is invested and grows to $10,565, which can be withdrawn tax-free.
- **Taxable account:** the same $3,120 grows to $10,565. The gain of $7,445 is taxed at the 15% long-term rate when sold, leaving around $9,449. With a low taxable income in retirement, the gain could even fall into the 0% bracket.

The figures compare tax treatments, not products. An account holding funds with high fees would shift the result considerably. The match outweighs every tax effect.

bloecke.md:
## What each leg is suited for

The numbering says nothing about the quality of a leg. Each one serves a different purpose.

- Social Security secures a base income for life. It pays through every market phase, rises with inflation and insures against [[Longevity risk|longevity risk]]. For most workers it is mandatory, and for many retirees it is the largest single source of income. Claiming later raises the monthly benefit permanently.
- Employer plans are worth using above all where the employer adds money. A match of 50% or 100% on your own deferral is an immediate return that no investment reliably offers. Without a match, what remains is the tax advantage, which depends on the tax rate today and in retirement and on the costs of the plan.
- Personal savings in a taxable account keep the money available. Only here can money be freely used before 59½, for example for a home, a business or a career break, without penalties or special rules. In return, income is taxed along the way.

For people with very low income and few assets, one rule outweighs any return assumption. Supplemental Security Income (SSI), the federal minimum income for people aged 65 or older or with disabilities, allows only $2,000 of countable resources for an individual and $3,000 for a couple. Retirement accounts count as resources if you can withdraw money from them, even with a penalty. Medicaid rules for long-term care differ from state to state. Savers who expect to rely on these programs should get advice before building up large account balances.

The leg and the account type determine when tax is paid and how tightly the money is tied up, but not how well it is invested. There are expensive and cheap investments in every account. Choosing the account and choosing the investment are two separate decisions. Over 30 years, fees and the employer match usually matter more than the choice between pre-tax and Roth.

A high tax rate today is a reason to consider pre-tax saving, but not a sufficient one. The deduction comes once, the restriction lasts until 59½. A saver who puts everything into a 401(k) at 35 and needs money at 45 pays income tax plus a 10% additional tax on early withdrawals unless an exception applies. A lower tax rate in retirement should not simply be assumed either. Required minimum distributions, the taxation of Social Security benefits and the death of a spouse, after which the survivor files as a single taxpayer, can push the rate up.

The Social Security Fairness Act of January 2025 repealed the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset. People with a pension from work not covered by Social Security, for example some teachers and police officers, no longer have their Social Security benefits reduced because of it. The law of 4 July 2025 known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Public Law 119-21) introduced an additional deduction of $6,000 for people aged 65 or older for the years 2025 to 2028, which phases out above $75,000 of income for single filers and $150,000 for joint filers. Social Security benefits themselves did not become tax-free. The same law created Trump accounts for children, which can receive contributions from 4 July 2026.

From 2026, under SECURE 2.0, catch-up contributions of employees whose wages in the previous year exceeded an indexed threshold must be made as Roth contributions. From 2027, the Saver's Credit is replaced by the Saver's Match, a federal matching contribution paid into the retirement account. The 2025 Social Security Trustees Report projects that the combined trust funds will be depleted in 2034, after which incoming taxes would cover around 81% of scheduled benefits unless Congress acts. There is no law on this so far.

mitnehmen: The three-legged stool describes US retirement income as Social Security, employer plans and personal savings; it is an image, not a legal category.
The tax code sorts money a second time into pre-tax, Roth and taxable; the more tax help an account offers, the more rules on access and withdrawals apply.
Pre-tax and Roth end with the same amount if the tax rate is the same today and in retirement; the advantage of either depends only on the difference between the two rates.
Social Security is mandatory, lifelong and adjusted for inflation, but it cannot be cashed out; 401(k) deferrals save income tax, but not Social Security and Medicare tax.
The sensible split depends on the employer match, the tax rate now and later, the need for access before 59½ and, for very low incomes, on the SSI resource limit.

begriffe.text: Common image of US retirement income as resting on Social Security, employer plans and personal savings. The term has no legal meaning, and its origin is unclear.

Account whose contributions reduce taxable income today and whose withdrawals are taxed in full as ordinary income, for example the Traditional 401(k) or a deductible Traditional IRA. Withdrawals before 59½ generally cost an additional 10% tax.

Account funded from taxed income whose qualified withdrawals, including all growth, are tax-free. Roth IRAs and, since 2024, Roth accounts in employer plans have no required minimum distributions for the owner.

Federal Insurance Contributions Act; the payroll taxes for Social Security (6.2% each for employee and employer up to $184,500 in 2026) and Medicare (1.45% each without a ceiling, plus 0.9% for the employee above $200,000 of wages). Deferrals to a 401(k) do not reduce them.

Means-tested federal benefit for people aged 65 or older, blind or with disabilities and with little income. Countable resources may not exceed $2,000 for an individual or $3,000 for a couple; retirement accounts count if money can be withdrawn from them.
